Results indicated that shelter/resilience hubs should provide priority access to charging powered mobility devices and potentially maintaining a community library of manual mobility devices. Although those with chronic mobility-limiting conditions had alternate devices and plans, a gap was found for individuals that may have temporary mobility issues (e.g., post-surgery, etc.). The remaining four community-based minimum resilience standards were based upon securing basic human needs during a disaster or grid outage. The Safety-Lighting standard focuses on preventing accidents and injuries during outages through adequate lighting equipment. This can be accomplished through battery-operated light sources and solar chargeable options. Community-based solutions included considering the temporary generators with outdoor lighting when street lighting is non-functional. This is an area where city-based infrastructure including solar lighting was recommended to the CIT. Essential for public safety, the Communication standard requires individuals to have connectivity (cellular or wifi) or a battery-powered radio to receive emergency alerts for the duration of an outage. Resilience hubs were identified as places for charging communication devices and key information dissemination points for community members. The Food Safety standard requires individuals to have access to three days of nonperishable food and mandates clear processes for replacing food impacted by power outages, especially for those dependent on food subsidies. Community-based solutions included the distribution of nonperishables, and cooking resources for perishables to mitigate food waste. Finally, the Water standard aligns with CDC recommendations of one gallon of water per person per day, requiring individuals to store water and potentially purification tablets, while mandating that the community establish a clear distribution plan for this resource in the event of grid outages with cascading impacts on the City’s water distribution system. 19 The community-based minimum resilient standards were vetted by the CIT and CSG, which passed them unanimously. From Tasks 1.0-3.0 a Community Energy Resilience Plan (CERP) was created and approved by CIT and CSG members. Duluth’s CERP includes a portfolio of solar and storage projects across the community that are shovel-ready based upon engineering and interconnection application completion. In addition to these five projects, additional solar-only options were prioritized based upon return on investment and ability to reduce blue sky energy costs.
